newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK PSBR to fall on healthy tax receipts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK PSBR to fall on healthy tax receipts.

text.p: The UK public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) is set to fall in April as economic growth continues to provide healthy tax receipts, analysts said.
"I think what you're seeing is very good progress on the receipts side, particularly with corporation tax," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
A Reuters consensus poll of analysts forecasts the government had to borrow 1.7 billion sterling to make up for the shortfall between tax receipts and spending compared with March's 8.8 billion stg.
The deficit is generally much larger than average in March as government departments rush to exhaust their budget before the end of the fiscal year.
April data are due at 0830 GMT on Monday.

And while higher tax receipts will help cut borrowing, a firmer hand on government spending has also allowed the PSBR to come in below expectations in recent months, a trend that should have continued in April.
"I think the surprise has been where departmental level spending has been controlled," said Stewart. "There was a degree of vigorous control of spending in 1996 and 1997."
The sell-off of another section of student loans and receipts from the sale of Ministry of Defence (MOD) houses added to the government's coffers in April.
"You are obviously going to get a benign impact from the receipts of the MOD housing stock and another tranche of the student loans book," said Stewart.
But some economists thought the government might have been forced to ease back on its tight spending policy in the run-up to the general election.

"Despite the fact that I think we are in for another revenue surprise given the strength of activity, I think it is conceivable that since it was the month before the election, there was some spending slippage," said Alex Garrard, European economist at UBS.

Economists agreed that spending commitments made by the Conservative government before the May 1 election had left Labour in a tricky position given the additional burden of its own spending commitments.

"I think generally the assumption will be that some special one-off effects in there have helped, but if the government is serious about meeting its deficit targets it can't simply rely on strong growth," said Garrard.

And while economists said the figures would have little impact on financial markets, barring a shock figure, the onus would be on the government to intervene on the tax side in the forthcoming budget.

"The consensus view I think is that Labour will not hit its spending targets and the difference will be made up on higher taxation," said Stewart. "I think Labour would quite like to respect the Maastricht fiscal criteria."
The Maastricht Treaty specifies the budget deficit should not exceed three percent of GDP for participation in European Economic and Monetary Union.
